items.stem: Which file traditionally stores local user account information (excluding passwords) on a Linux system?

options.rationale: Correct: /etc/passwd holds user account entries; hashed passwords live in /etc/shadow.
/etc/hostname stores the system hostname, not user accounts.
/etc/fstab describes filesystems to mount, not user accounts.
/etc/crontab defines scheduled jobs, not user accounts.

items.explanation: Correct: /etc/passwd holds user account entries; hashed passwords live in /etc/shadow.

items.stem: What is the primary purpose of cron on a Linux system?

options.text: Run commands automatically on a recurring schedule
options.rationale: Correct: cron executes jobs at scheduled times defined in crontabs.
Package management is handled by apt/dpkg or yum/rpm, not cron.
Network configuration uses tools like ip or NetworkManager, not cron.
Encryption is handled by tools such as LUKS, not cron.

items.explanation: Correct: cron executes jobs at scheduled times defined in crontabs.

items.stem: Select TWO practices that improve SSH server security.

options.text: Disabling direct root login over SSH
options.rationale: Correct: disabling root login reduces the risk of a high-value brute-force target.

options.text: Using key-based authentication instead of passwords
options.rationale: Correct: key-based auth is stronger than reusable passwords.
Empty passwords are a serious security weakness.

options.text: Running the SSH daemon as every user simultaneously
options.rationale: This is not a real or meaningful configuration.

options.text: Sharing one private key among all administrators
options.rationale: Shared private keys remove accountability and increase risk.

items.explanation: Correct: disabling root login reduces the risk of a high-value brute-force target.
